units.title: Signal Fundamentals
units.tip: A signal is any information that varies over time or space. Signals can be continuous (defined at every moment) or discrete (defined only at certain points). Understanding how to represent and classify signals is essential for signal processing.

exercises.question: What is a continuous signal?
exercises.answer: A signal defined at every point in time
exercises.explain: A continuous signal, denoted x(t), has a value for every real number t. Sound waves, temperature, and voltage in a circuit are continuous signals.
choices: A signal defined only at integer times
A signal defined at every point in time
A signal with a single value
A signal that never changes

exercises.question: What is a discrete signal?
exercises.answer: A signal defined only at certain points in time
exercises.explain: A discrete signal, denoted x[n], is defined only at discrete time points, usually integers. Digital music samples and sensor readings taken at intervals are discrete signals.
choices: A signal defined only at certain points in time
A signal with infinite values
A signal that repeats forever
A signal that is always zero

exercises.question: What is sampling?
exercises.answer: Converting a continuous signal into a discrete signal by measuring it at regular intervals
exercises.explain: Sampling measures a continuous signal at specific times. The sample rate is the number of samples per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
choices: Converting a continuous signal into a discrete signal by measuring it at regular intervals
Creating a digital copy of a signal
Amplifying a weak signal
Smoothing a noisy signal

exercises.question: What is a sample?
exercises.answer: A single measurement value of a signal at a specific time
exercises.explain: A sample is one data point taken from a signal at a particular instant. When collected regularly, samples form a discrete signal.
choices: A type of filter
A frequency component
The average of all signal values
A single measurement value of a signal at a specific time

exercises.question: What is the relationship between sampling interval and sample rate?
exercises.answer: Sample rate is the reciprocal of the sampling interval
exercises.explain: If the sampling interval is T seconds, the sample rate is f_s = 1/T samples per second. A 44 kHz sample rate means samples every 1/44000 seconds.
choices: They are the same thing
Sample rate is the reciprocal of the sampling interval
They are independent
Sample interval is always larger

exercises.question: What is a periodic signal?
exercises.answer: A signal that repeats its pattern after a fixed time interval
exercises.explain: A signal x(t) is periodic with period T if x(t) = x(t + T) for all t. The smallest such T is called the fundamental period.
choices: A signal that repeats its pattern after a fixed time interval
A signal with zero average value
A signal that only increases
A signal that oscillates between two values

exercises.question: What is the period of a signal?
exercises.answer: The time required for the signal to complete one full cycle
exercises.explain: The period T is the smallest time such that the signal repeats. The sinusoid sin(2*pi*f*t) has period T = 1/f.
choices: The average value of the signal
The rate of change of the signal
The time required for the signal to complete one full cycle
The maximum value of the signal

exercises.question: What is a sinusoidal signal?
exercises.answer: A signal of the form A*sin(2*pi*f*t + phi) or A*cos(2*pi*f*t + phi)
exercises.explain: Sinusoids are the most important periodic signals. They are defined by amplitude A, frequency f, and phase phi.
choices: A signal that is always positive
A signal with a constant value
A signal of the form A*sin(2*pi*f*t + phi) or A*cos(2*pi*f*t + phi)
A signal that changes randomly

exercises.question: What is the amplitude of a sinusoid?
exercises.answer: The maximum distance the signal reaches from its center value
exercises.explain: Amplitude A determines the size of the oscillation. A larger amplitude means bigger swings from the center.
choices: The number of cycles per second
The maximum distance the signal reaches from its center value
The average value of the signal
The angle offset of the signal

exercises.question: What is an aperiodic signal?
exercises.answer: A signal that does not repeat after any fixed time interval
exercises.explain: Aperiodic signals have no repeating pattern. Examples include random noise, a single pulse, and a chirp (swept frequency signal).
choices: A signal that does not repeat after any fixed time interval
A signal that repeats slowly
A signal that only exists for a short time
A signal with very low amplitude

units.title: Frequency and Phase
units.tip: Frequency describes how fast a signal oscillates. Phase describes where in the cycle the signal is at a given moment. Both are fundamental to understanding signal behavior and signal processing.

exercises.question: What is the frequency of a signal?
exercises.answer: The number of cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz)
exercises.explain: Frequency f tells how many complete oscillations occur in one second. A 1 Hz signal completes one cycle per second.
choices: The maximum value of the signal
The number of cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz)
The time for one cycle
The rate of change of the signal

exercises.question: What is angular frequency?
exercises.answer: The frequency in radians per second, denoted omega
exercises.explain: Angular frequency omega = 2*pi*f relates to ordinary frequency by a factor of 2*pi. It is used in the exponential form of sinusoids.
choices: The total angle the signal sweeps
The frequency measured in cycles per second
The frequency in radians per second, denoted omega
The phase of the signal

exercises.question: What is the relationship between frequency and period?
exercises.answer: Frequency is the reciprocal of period: f = 1/T
exercises.explain: If a signal has period T seconds, it repeats T times per second, so frequency f = 1/T. A period of 0.5 seconds means frequency of 2 Hz.
choices: f = 2*pi*T
Frequency is the reciprocal of period: f = 1/T
They are independent
f = T

exercises.question: What is the frequency of a sinusoid with period T = 4 seconds?
exercises.answer: 0.25 hertz
exercises.explain: f = 1/T = 1/4 = 0.25 Hz. This sinusoid completes one quarter of a cycle per second.
choices: 8 hertz
2 hertz
0.25 hertz
4 hertz

exercises.question: What is the angular frequency omega of a signal with frequency f = 10 Hz?
exercises.answer: 20*pi radians per second (approximately 62.8 rad/s)
exercises.explain: omega = 2*pi*f = 2*pi*10 = 20*pi rad/s. This is approximately 62.8 rad/s.
choices: 100 radians per second
5 radians per second
10 radians per second
20*pi radians per second (approximately 62.8 rad/s)

exercises.question: What is phase of a sinusoidal signal?
exercises.answer: The angle offset that determines where in the cycle the signal starts
exercises.explain: Phase phi (in degrees or radians) shifts the signal left or right in time. sin(t) has zero phase, while sin(t + pi/2) has a pi/2 phase shift.
choices: The rate of change at time zero
The frequency of the signal
The maximum value of the signal
The angle offset that determines where in the cycle the signal starts

exercises.question: What does a phase shift of pi/2 radians represent?
exercises.answer: A quarter-cycle delay or advance
exercises.explain: pi/2 radians is 90 degrees. A phase shift of pi/2 means the signal starts 90 degrees (one quarter of 360) ahead or behind.
choices: A full cycle
A quarter-cycle delay or advance
Half a cycle
No change

exercises.question: What is phase difference between two signals?
exercises.answer: The angle difference between them at any given time
exercises.explain: If signal 1 is sin(t) and signal 2 is sin(t + phi), the phase difference is phi. When phi = 0, they are in phase. When phi = pi, they are out of phase.
choices: The difference in their amplitudes
The angle difference between them at any given time
How much one is louder than the other
The difference in their frequencies

exercises.question: When are two sinusoids in phase?
exercises.answer: When their phase difference is zero or a multiple of 2*pi
exercises.explain: In-phase sinusoids reach their peaks and zeros at the same times. This happens when the phase difference is 0, 2*pi, 4*pi, etc.
choices: When one has zero amplitude
When they have different frequencies
When they have the same amplitude
When their phase difference is zero or a multiple of 2*pi

exercises.question: When are two sinusoids completely out of phase?
exercises.answer: When their phase difference is pi or an odd multiple of pi
exercises.explain: Out-of-phase sinusoids are opposite: when one peaks, the other reaches its minimum. A phase difference of pi, 3*pi, 5*pi, etc. gives complete cancellation when the amplitudes are equal.
choices: When their phase difference is pi or an odd multiple of pi
When they have the same phase
When one is much larger
When they have the same frequency

units.title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems
units.tip: A system is linear if it obeys superposition: the response to a sum of inputs equals the sum of responses to each input. A system is time-invariant if delaying the input only delays the output by the same amount. Most natural and engineered systems are approximately LTI.

exercises.question: What is a linear system?
exercises.answer: A system where the output for a sum of inputs equals the sum of outputs
exercises.explain: Linearity means y_1(t) + y_2(t) = y(x_1(t) + x_2(t)). This allows decomposing complex signals into simpler ones.
choices: A system where the output for a sum of inputs equals the sum of outputs
A system that does not saturate
A system with a straight-line graph
A system whose output is always larger than its input

exercises.question: What is a time-invariant system?
exercises.answer: A system where delaying the input also delays the output by the same amount
exercises.explain: In a time-invariant system, the relationship between input and output does not change over time. A circuit with fixed resistors is time-invariant.
choices: A system where delaying the input also delays the output by the same amount
A system with a time-varying transfer function
A system that depends on the current time
A system that changes over time

exercises.question: What is an LTI (Linear Time-Invariant) system?
exercises.answer: A system that is both linear and time-invariant
exercises.explain: LTI systems are the most important class in signal processing. They can be completely described by their impulse response.
choices: A system that only works at one frequency
A system with nonlinear elements
A system that is both linear and time-invariant
A system with time-varying parameters

exercises.question: What is causality in a system?
exercises.answer: The output depends only on past and present inputs, not future inputs
exercises.explain: A causal system is physically realizable. It cannot respond to events that have not yet occurred.
choices: The system causes all effects
The input causes the output
The output depends only on past and present inputs, not future inputs
The system runs backwards in time

exercises.question: What is stability in a system?
exercises.answer: Bounded inputs produce bounded outputs
exercises.explain: A stable system (BIBO: bounded-input bounded-output) never produces an output that grows without bound from a bounded input. Unstable systems can blow up.
choices: The system never changes
The system has zero error
The system is at equilibrium
Bounded inputs produce bounded outputs

exercises.question: What is an impulse signal?
exercises.answer: A signal that is zero everywhere except at one point in time
exercises.explain: The impulse (delta function) is infinitely tall and infinitely narrow, with unit area. It represents an instantaneous input.
choices: A signal that alternates
A long-duration signal
A signal with constant value
A signal that is zero everywhere except at one point in time

exercises.question: What is impulse response?
exercises.answer: The output of a system when the input is an impulse
exercises.explain: The impulse response h(t) completely characterizes an LTI system. Given h(t) and any input, we can compute the output using convolution.
choices: The output of a system when the input is an impulse
The frequency response of the system
How the system responds to all inputs
The gain at DC

exercises.question: What is the step response of a system?
exercises.answer: The output when the input is a unit step function
exercises.explain: The step response shows how the system settles to a new condition when given a constant input. It reveals rise time, overshoot, and settling time.
choices: How many steps the input takes
The time derivative of the input
The frequency response
The output when the input is a unit step function

exercises.question: How are impulse response and step response related?
exercises.answer: The step response is the integral (cumulative sum) of the impulse response
exercises.explain: If h(t) is impulse response, then integrating h from negative infinity to time t gives the step response. Conversely, the derivative of step response is impulse response.
choices: The step response is the integral (cumulative sum) of the impulse response
The impulse response is the integral of step response
They are unrelated
They are the same thing

exercises.question: Why is knowing the impulse response useful?
exercises.answer: Because it completely determines the system's output for any input signal
exercises.explain: For LTI systems, convolution of the impulse response with any input gives the output. This makes impulse response the most important system property.
choices: Because it completely determines the system's output for any input signal
It is just historical tradition
It tells the frequency response only
It is easier to measure than other properties

units.title: Convolution and Filtering
units.tip: Convolution is the mathematical operation that combines an input signal with a system's impulse response to produce the output. Filtering shapes a signal by attenuating or amplifying certain frequencies.

exercises.question: What is convolution?
exercises.answer: The mathematical operation combining input and impulse response to produce output
exercises.explain: Convolution is denoted y(t) = x(t) * h(t). It represents how the system's memory and structure shapes the input signal.
choices: The Fourier transform of a signal
Multiplying two signals together
Filtering high frequencies
The mathematical operation combining input and impulse response to produce output

exercises.question: What does the convolution integral compute?
exercises.answer: For each output time t, it sums the weighted input values, weighted by h(t - tau)
exercises.explain: y(t) = integral of x(tau) * h(t - tau) d(tau). This weights each past input by how far it is in the past (reflected in the impulse response).
choices: For each output time t, it sums the weighted input values, weighted by h(t - tau)
The energy of the signal
The frequency content
The Fourier series of the signal

exercises.question: What is discrete convolution?
exercises.answer: Convolution for discrete-time signals, using summation instead of integration
exercises.explain: For discrete signals: y[n] = sum of x[k] * h[n - k]. It computes output samples as weighted sums of past input samples.
choices: Convolution for discrete-time signals, using summation instead of integration
Convolution that never converges
Convolution only for periodic signals
Sampling a continuous convolution

exercises.question: Is convolution commutative?
exercises.answer: Yes, x(t) * h(t) = h(t) * x(t)
exercises.explain: Convolution is commutative, meaning the order does not matter. This is mathematically true and reflects that input and system can be swapped.
choices: Only at certain frequencies
Only for even-length signals
No, order always matters
Yes, x(t) * h(t) = h(t) * x(t)

exercises.question: What is the computational cost of discrete convolution for N-point signals?
exercises.answer: Approximately N^2 operations
exercises.explain: Direct convolution requires N^2 multiplications and additions. Fast algorithms using FFT reduce this to N*log(N).
choices: N*log(N) for all cases
N operations
Approximately N^2 operations
2^N operations

exercises.question: What is a filter?
exercises.answer: A system that selectively attenuates or amplifies signals at different frequencies
exercises.explain: Filters process signals based on frequency content. A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones; a high-pass filter does the opposite.
choices: A device that amplifies all frequencies equally
A device that removes all frequencies
A system that selectively attenuates or amplifies signals at different frequencies
Something that cleans water only

exercises.question: What is a low-pass filter?
exercises.answer: A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies
exercises.explain: A low-pass filter has a cutoff frequency. Frequencies below cutoff pass with little attenuation; frequencies above are strongly attenuated.
choices: A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies
A filter that only works with analog signals
A filter that removes all frequencies
A filter that passes high frequencies

exercises.question: What is a high-pass filter?
exercises.answer: A filter that passes high frequencies and attenuates low frequencies
exercises.explain: A high-pass filter passes signals above its cutoff frequency and blocks those below. It removes DC and low-frequency components.
choices: A filter that passes low frequencies
A filter that passes all frequencies
A filter made only from resistors
A filter that passes high frequencies and attenuates low frequencies

exercises.question: What is a cutoff frequency?
exercises.answer: The frequency where the filter transitions from passing to blocking
exercises.explain: At the cutoff frequency, the gain is typically 0.707 times the passband gain (or 3 dB down). This marks the edge of the filter's passband.
choices: The frequency that the filter completely blocks
The frequency where the filter transitions from passing to blocking
The Nyquist frequency
The highest frequency in the universe

exercises.question: What is a band-pass filter?
exercises.answer: A filter that passes a range of frequencies and attenuates frequencies outside that range
exercises.explain: A band-pass filter has a lower and upper cutoff frequency. Frequencies between them pass; frequencies outside are blocked.
choices: A filter that passes only the lowest frequencies
A filter made from two resistors
A filter that passes a range of frequencies and attenuates frequencies outside that range
A filter that passes only the highest frequencies

units.title: Fourier Analysis
units.tip: Fourier analysis decomposes any signal into a sum of sinusoids at different frequencies. The Fourier series works for periodic signals, while the Fourier transform works for all signals. This reveals the frequency content of signals.

exercises.question: What is the Fourier series?
exercises.answer: A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of sinusoids at harmonic frequencies
exercises.explain: Any periodic signal can be written as a DC component plus sinusoids at frequencies f, 2f, 3f, etc. (multiples of the fundamental frequency).
choices: A formula for calculating frequency
A method to solve differential equations
A technique used only in music
A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of sinusoids at harmonic frequencies

exercises.question: What is the fundamental frequency in a Fourier series?
exercises.answer: The frequency of the periodic signal itself (1/T)
exercises.explain: If the signal has period T, the fundamental frequency is f_0 = 1/T. All other frequency components are integer multiples of this.
choices: Always 60 Hz
The highest frequency in the signal
The Nyquist frequency
The frequency of the periodic signal itself (1/T)

exercises.question: What are harmonics in a Fourier series?
exercises.answer: Sinusoids at integer multiples of the fundamental frequency
exercises.explain: The first harmonic (fundamental) is at f_0, the second at 2*f_0, the third at 3*f_0, and so on. Each harmonic contributes to the shape.
choices: Sounds that are pleasing to hear
Only even-frequency components
Sinusoids at integer multiples of the fundamental frequency
The loudness of a signal

exercises.question: What does a Fourier coefficient tell you?
exercises.answer: The amplitude and phase of each sinusoid in the decomposition
exercises.explain: The Fourier coefficients describe how much of each harmonic frequency is present in the signal. Larger coefficients mean stronger contributions.
choices: The amplitude and phase of each sinusoid in the decomposition
Whether the signal is periodic
The duration of the signal
The total energy in the signal

exercises.question: Why is the Fourier series useful?
exercises.answer: It reveals which frequencies are present and their relative strengths
exercises.explain: By decomposing a signal into sinusoids, we learn its frequency content. This is crucial for understanding signal behavior and designing filters.
choices: It simplifies the differential equations only
It reveals which frequencies are present and their relative strengths
It changes the fundamental frequency
It makes signals shorter

exercises.question: What is the Fourier transform?
exercises.answer: A mathematical operation that converts a signal from the time domain to the frequency domain
exercises.explain: The Fourier transform X(f) shows what frequencies are present in signal x(t). It works for aperiodic signals, where Fourier series only work for periodic ones.
choices: A method to invert a matrix
A series of sinusoids only
A mathematical operation that converts a signal from the time domain to the frequency domain
A technique for amplifying signals

exercises.question: What is the frequency spectrum?
exercises.answer: The magnitude and phase information of a signal at each frequency
exercises.explain: The magnitude spectrum |X(f)| shows how much of each frequency is present. The phase spectrum tells the phase angle of each component.
choices: The range of frequencies a device can handle
Only the positive frequencies
The magnitude and phase information of a signal at each frequency
The total power in the signal

exercises.question: What is frequency response of a system?
exercises.answer: The gain and phase shift applied by the system at each frequency
exercises.explain: Frequency response H(f) describes how the system treats each frequency component. It is the Fourier transform of the impulse response.
choices: How fast the system works
How often the system updates
The gain and phase shift applied by the system at each frequency
The range of input frequencies

exercises.question: How do you find the output of an LTI system using Fourier transforms?
exercises.answer: Multiply the input spectrum by the frequency response, then inverse transform
exercises.explain: Y(f) = X(f) * H(f), then y(t) is found by inverse Fourier transform. Multiplication in frequency domain equals convolution in time domain.
choices: Multiply the input spectrum by the frequency response, then inverse transform
No multiplication is needed
Add the input spectrum to the frequency response
Divide the input spectrum by the frequency response

exercises.question: What is the magnitude response of a filter?
exercises.answer: The gain (amplitude scaling) at each frequency
exercises.explain: Magnitude response |H(f)| tells how much each frequency component is amplified or attenuated. It does not include phase information.
choices: The phase shift at each frequency
The input signal spectrum
The gain (amplitude scaling) at each frequency
The time-domain impulse response

units.title: Sampling and Aliasing
units.tip: Sampling converts continuous signals to discrete ones. The Nyquist rate determines the minimum sampling frequency needed to avoid losing information. Aliasing occurs when sampling is too slow, causing high frequencies to appear as low ones.

exercises.question: What is the Nyquist sampling theorem?
exercises.answer: A signal is perfectly reconstructible if sampled above twice its highest frequency
exercises.explain: If a signal has highest frequency f_max, the sample rate must exceed 2*f_max. The value 2*f_max is called the Nyquist rate.
choices: A signal must be sampled at least once per cycle
All signals need sampling at 44 kHz
Sampling rate does not matter
A signal is perfectly reconstructible if sampled above twice its highest frequency

exercises.question: What is the Nyquist frequency?
exercises.answer: Half the sampling rate; the highest frequency that can be represented
exercises.explain: If sampling at f_s, the Nyquist frequency is f_N = f_s/2. No frequency above this can be accurately represented.
choices: The highest frequency in the signal
The frequency of the sampling clock
Half the sampling rate; the highest frequency that can be represented
Twice the sampling rate

exercises.question: For a signal with maximum frequency 5 kHz, what is the minimum sampling rate?
exercises.answer: 10 kHz
exercises.explain: f_s = 2*f_max = 2*5 kHz = 10 kHz. Sampling at exactly 10 kHz is the theoretical minimum (in practice, sample slightly faster).
choices: 20 kHz
2.5 kHz
5 kHz
10 kHz

exercises.question: What is the Nyquist frequency for audio sampled at 44 kHz?
exercises.answer: 22 kHz
exercises.explain: f_N = f_s/2 = 44 kHz / 2 = 22 kHz. This is slightly above the human hearing range (typically up to 20 kHz).
choices: 44 kHz
22 kHz
11 kHz
88 kHz

exercises.question: Can a signal be perfectly reconstructed from its samples?
exercises.answer: Yes, if the Nyquist rate is satisfied and an ideal low-pass filter is used
exercises.explain: Perfect reconstruction requires meeting the Nyquist criterion and filtering to remove frequency copies. Ideal filters do not exist in practice.
choices: Yes, if the Nyquist rate is satisfied and an ideal low-pass filter is used
Never, sampling always loses information
Only for periodic signals
Only for very short signals

exercises.question: What is aliasing?
exercises.answer: High frequencies appearing as lower frequencies when sampling is too slow
exercises.explain: When f_s < 2*f_max, high-frequency components fold back into the baseband. A 25 kHz signal sampled at 44 kHz appears as a 19 kHz signal.
choices: High frequencies appearing as lower frequencies when sampling is too slow
Multiple signals being sampled together
The process of sampling a signal
Applying an alias to a function

exercises.question: Why is aliasing a problem?
exercises.answer: It causes high-frequency information to be lost and misrepresented as lower frequencies
exercises.explain: Aliased frequencies cannot be separated from true signal components after sampling. The information is permanently corrupted.
choices: It has no negative effect
It increases the sampling rate
It causes high-frequency information to be lost and misrepresented as lower frequencies
It makes the signal louder

exercises.question: What is an anti-aliasing filter?
exercises.answer: A low-pass filter applied before sampling to remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency
exercises.explain: An anti-aliasing filter prevents aliasing by eliminating high-frequency components before sampling. It is a critical component in analog-to-digital conversion.
choices: A filter that amplifies high frequencies
A filter applied after sampling
A filter that removes low frequencies
A low-pass filter applied before sampling to remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency

exercises.question: How does an anti-aliasing filter prevent aliasing?
exercises.answer: By attenuating frequencies above the Nyquist frequency before they can be sampled
exercises.explain: If all frequency components above f_N are removed before sampling at f_s = 2*f_N, no aliasing can occur.
choices: By increasing the sampling rate
By removing low frequencies
By amplifying the signal
By attenuating frequencies above the Nyquist frequency before they can be sampled

exercises.question: What cutoff frequency should an anti-aliasing filter have?
exercises.answer: The Nyquist frequency (half the sampling rate)
exercises.explain: The anti-aliasing filter's cutoff should be at f_s/2 to allow all valid frequencies (below Nyquist) while removing problematic ones above.
choices: Twice the sampling rate
The Nyquist frequency (half the sampling rate)
10 times the lowest frequency
The signal's center frequency
